text: Each map holds 537 bomb hits. One is pure chance, the other follows a rule. Which is chance? In 1944, Londoners claimed flying bombs fell in clusters, and precise aim would put factories at risk. Build the detector your eye is running. Cut each map into 576 squares, and flag any square with three or more hits, like this one. Map A lights up with 39 targets, map B with none. So A looks aimed. Backwards. I dropped every hit on map A at random, so all 39 targets are false alarms. Map B's rule, no two hits closer than four-fifths of a square. Your eye, like the detector, expects chance to look that even. Each bomb has a one in five 76 chance of landing in this square. To stay empty, all 537 must miss. Guess how many squares stay empty? About 227. Map A has 222. Those empty squares force pileups. 183 hits must land where another already did. Let's call the average hits per square lambda. One minus a small slice raised to a big power is e to the minus lambda, almost exactly, Call that p of 0. For two hits in the square, pick two bombs. 537 times 536 ways, over 2, since each pair counts twice. Each has that same chance, and the rest miss. E to the minus lambda again 536 is almost 537 For three hits each two becomes a 3 For any k a k The powers merge into lambda to the k the Poisson distribution. Times 576 squares, it predicts these purple bars. The honest detector compares whole histograms. 39 targets, and chance predicts 39. The chi-squared misfit squares each bar's gap bars gap and divides by chance's bar because short bars wobble less. A miss on a short bar counts more. Map A scores. 2.0. Three out of four simulated chance maps score worse. That share P is .74. Now map B. Half the expected empty squares, a tower of single hits, misfit 272. A pattern this even is the fingerprint of a spacing rule. Aimed bombs would miss the other way. Extra empty squares, extra pileups. In 1946, R. D. Clarke published the same test on London's real hits. 537 in 576 squares. Chance predicted 227 empty squares. Clarke counted 229. Overall, p equals .88. London's clusters were no sign of precise aim. The bombs were aimed at central London, but tended to fall short, so farther north, hits were about half as dense. Score the north alone and it fits chance too, p equals .45. The aim hides in lambda, which the test holds fixed. The clumps in map A are what no aim at all looks like if you chose map B. You chose the rule.
